body.heading: Big celebrations are rare; small wins are daily
paragraphs: Families tend to mark the summits — exams passed, jobs landed, birthdays — and let the foothills pass silently. But most of a life is foothills: the first solo bike ride to the corner, the difficult phone call made, the week of early nights kept. A household that notices small wins has something to celebrate most days.
Noticing is the skill. It requires no budget, only attention: the report at dinner that begins 'tell us one thing that went right today'.

body.heading: Ways to mark a small win
paragraphs: Keep the rituals tiny and quick: a particular cheer, a dessert that appears, the win written on a slip and dropped in a jar on the shelf. The jar fills over a year and becomes the best possible reading on a flat evening in December.
Match the celebration to the person. One child wants an audience and a drumroll; another wants a quiet word and no fuss at all. Celebrating someone in their own language is itself the gift.

body.heading: Include the nearly-wins
paragraphs: Effort that fell short deserves its share of the ritual — the race lost well, the audition that did not land. A family that only celebrates outcomes teaches its members to hide their attempts; one that honours effort makes trying safe.
Keep the celebrations proportionate and frequent rather than rare and enormous. A family fluent in small celebrations rarely has to manufacture a big one.
